title: snapshot edgeValue drops the ADR-0021 relation qualifiers the projection deliberately carries, so lore changed and lore provenance cannot answer what ADR-0021 exists to answer
description:
Raised by opum-agent's investigation 6 under OPAG-204, re-confirmed by opum-doc, and measured
AGAIN here against lore-cli origin/dev (c99e1d77) before filing -- two sessions had reported the
line numbers and neither of them is this repository.

CONFIRMED VERBATIM, all against origin/dev:

- src/core/snapshot.ts:490 `edgeValue` copies from, to, kind, target, ordinal, dangling,
  workspaceFromKind, workspaceToKind, workspaceLinkKind -- and none of `statement`, `version`,
  `relationOrdinal`.
- src/core/snapshot.ts:166 `edgeValueSchema`, .strict() at line 178, carries none of the three
  either, so they cannot be added without a `lore-retained-snapshot/2`.

TWO THINGS THIS REPOSITORY CAN ADD THAT NEITHER REPORTING SESSION HAD.

1. THE ADR CARRIED "whether the omission was deliberate" AS AN OPEN QUESTION. It is answerable,
   and the answer is in this repo's own source. `ProjectionEdgeRecord`
   (src/core/ladybug-source.ts:140) declares the three fields under an explicit comment:
   "ADR-0021 relation qualifiers, carried verbatim so an indexed read is as precise as a direct
   one." The stated intent of the fields is to be carried verbatim. `edgeValue` is the one place
   that does not carry them. That is a defect against written intent, not a deliberate projection
   choice. Recorded so the open question closes on evidence rather than staying open by default.

2. HOW IT SURVIVED, which is the object-identity split this fleet keeps naming. `relationOrdinal`
   IS covered by tests -- test/indexed-retrieval.test.ts and test/relations.test.ts. It is absent
   from test/snapshot.test.ts and test/snapshot-command.test.ts entirely. So the suite proves the
   PROJECTION carries the qualifiers and nothing anywhere asserts the SNAPSHOT preserves them. A
   reader grepping the suite for `relationOrdinal` finds coverage and concludes it is covered. The
   object measured is the projection; the object the conclusion is about is the retained snapshot.

CHECKED AND NOT A DEFECT, recorded so nobody re-reports it: `edgeValue` also omits
`workspaceSourceRecordKey`, which looks like a fourth instance and is not one -- it is consumed at
src/core/snapshot.ts:459 to build the provenance record rather than stored on the edge. Three
omissions, not four.

CONSEQUENCE (opum-doc's framing, which this repo agrees with on its own reading): `lore changed`
can never report a relation re-pin, and `lore provenance` cannot recover which `claim_version` was
cited at a past snapshot -- exactly the question ADR-0021 exists to answer.

FIX SHAPE, not prescribed: adding three fields to a .strict() schema is a schema version bump, so
this needs `lore-retained-snapshot/2` and a decision about reading existing /1 snapshots (which
genuinely do not contain the data -- a migration cannot invent it, so a /1 snapshot should report
the qualifiers as UNKNOWN rather than as absent; inferring absence from a missing field is the
same error as reading a dated snapshot as present tense). SEQUENCE THIS AGAINST ODOC-231's
committed-citation design before building it: if a snapshot becomes a citation plus a projection
digest rather than a stored projection, the qualifiers come back from re-deriving at the cited
commit and the schema bump may land differently or not at all. Do not fix it in isolation first.

Source design record: opum-doc ODOC-231,
docs/adr/ground-lore-version-control-in-git-with-committed-citations-and-a-derived-index.md, read
here from opum-doc origin/dev at 843768c72684fa2b5c046cf1547b3bf628c4a605 on 2026-09-18.
implementationNotes:
ORCHESTRATOR RULINGS, opum-agent (OPAG-212) 2026-09-18, relayed. NOT YET BINDING: a relay binds
when opum-doc lands the amendment to ODOC-231 on main; read it there before building against it.
Recorded now so the thread survives, flagged so it is not mistaken for a landed decision.

RULING: the "whether the omission was deliberate" open question is CLOSED as a defect against
written intent, citing this record. opum-agent re-verified this repository's source independently
via the GitHub API at c99e1d77 rather than accepting the analysis, and added evidence stronger
than the comment alone: the WORKSPACE-ONLY endpoint fields declared directly BENEATH the ADR-0021
qualifiers in ProjectionEdgeRecord, under their own comment, ARE carried by edgeValue. The author
carried the fields they were thinking about and missed the block above. An asymmetry within one
type declaration is harder to read as deliberate than a flat omission.

A SECOND INSTANCE OF THE SAME REGRESSION, found by opum-agent while verifying and measured here:
ODOC-231 section 2 specifies a flat `.lore/snapshots/<name>.json`. Measured against origin/dev,
today's layout is
  .lore/cache/snapshots/1/<kind>/<digestHex(scopeKey)>/<digestHex(snapshotKey)>.json
from SNAPSHOT_CACHE_REL_ROOT (snapshot-store.ts:29) plus scopePath (233-237) and snapshotPath
(239-241). The flat form drops FOUR dimensions, not the one the ruling named: the format-version
segment `1`, the scope kind, the scope key, and the digest filename.

The version segment is the one that would hurt most if discovered mid-build. It is already how a
lore-retained-snapshot/2 store would coexist with /1 on disk instead of migrating in place. A flat
committed path has no such segment, so a future lore-committed-citation/2 would either break /1
readers in place or invent the segment retroactively -- after the files are committed in
consumers' repositories, which is exactly when a path change stops being cheap.

Related: the path/identity guard at snapshot-store.ts:150-155 throws "retained snapshot path and
embedded identity disagree" on a mismatch of scopeKind, scopeKey OR snapshotKey. A flat path does
not weaken that guard, it removes the substrate for all three of its assertions.

DESIGN TENSION RAISED BACK TO THE ORCHESTRATOR, not decided here: every path segment today is a
digest, and a committed citation wants a human-readable name because reviewability in a pull
request is the whole point. Those conflict. A human-chosen name in a committed path is new attack
and portability surface an uncommitted cache never had -- traversal, case-insensitive collision on
macOS and Windows, Unicode normalization differing between the writing machine and the reviewing
one, length limits. Recommended: human name as the filename, validated hard at creation against a
narrow charset, with the machine-derived scope segments left digested.

ALSO RAISED BACK, with a measurement: canonicalRepositoryRoot (snapshot-store.ts:268) resolves and
realpaths the INVOCATION root, so a workspace snapshot lands in the .lore/ of whichever member
repo the command ran in. Recommended that this stay non-intrinsic -- making it intrinsic needs a
primary member, which does not exist (workspace-projection.ts:64 orders members by memberId and
gives none primacy). The cost to design for: the same workspace citation taken from two member
repos yields two committed files, both valid, neither aware of the other, with identical scope
keys so scope-keying does not detect it. Recommended fix is to have the citation record the member
it was taken in, making a duplicate detectable by comparison rather than invisible.

CARRIED HERE FROM THE THREAD so it does not live only in a message: removing the retention cap has
to remove BOTH sites -- SNAPSHOT_RETENTION_LIMIT (snapshot.ts:19) and the hardcoded `maximum: 16`
at commands/snapshot.ts:77 that does not read the constant -- or `lore snapshot list` keeps
reporting a bound that no longer exists. Belongs to the record retiring the retention contract.

STATUS CORRECTION, 2026-09-18: the rulings recorded in the note above ARE NOW BINDING. The note
marked them "NOT YET BINDING" correctly at the time; Amendment 1 (ODOC-232) has since landed on
opum-doc main at 2785f9f5fdffa2a9a4e34f8be3a38815e1e7b90a. Verified here rather than accepted from
the relay: opum-doc main == dev == 2785f9f.

Also verified rather than accepted: the amendment does not disturb what was already measured
against. Section 2 of the ADR is BYTE-IDENTICAL between 843768c7 (the ref this repo first read)
and 2785f9f -- confirmed by hashing the section at both refs, both
dd5456c7af3560e339386538dbaa428e76f779c583ecb7a66b3ece19912da55a. The file is not purely additive
(10 lines removed), but every removal is ruling 3 being applied: the Downstream-records defect
bullet rewritten to cite this task, and the "was the omission deliberate" open question deleted
because it is closed. Recording the distinction because "the file is additive" and "section 2 is
unchanged" are different claims about different objects, and only the second one is true.

WHAT THE AMENDMENT ADDS BEYOND THE RELAY, read from main rather than from messages. opum-doc
corrected the orchestrator's relay twice while recording it, and both corrections change what an
implementer should build:

- The relay said sections 2 and 5 "reach opposite conclusions" on the unverifiable case. They do
  not: section 5 decides it, section 2 is SILENT on it. The distinction matters because silence is
  the more dangerous failure -- a contradiction gets caught by a reader holding both sections,
  whereas an omission reads as a complete specification and gets implemented as two outcomes by
  someone doing nothing wrong.
- The relay called the dropped path dimension "the member dimension". It is the SCOPE dimension:
  scopePath is keyed by scope kind and scope key, a workspace's scope key is the workspace key
  rather than a member id, and members never appear in the path at all. Building to the relay's
  wording would send an implementer looking for a per-member directory level that does not exist.

And one point opum-doc raised that neither this repo nor the orchestrator did: do NOT restore the
scope dimension by copying scopePath wholesale. snapshotPath names leaves by digestHex(snapshotKey),
while a committed citation's filename is human on purpose -- reviewability in a pull request is the
whole reason a committed citation beats the cache, and a 64-hex filename is not reviewable. The
scope dimension returns; digest-named leaves do not follow it in.

NAMING EVIDENCE FOR THE MANDATORY-HYPHEN QUESTION (opum-agent's open question under OPAG-212,
asked 2026-09-18). Recorded here rather than only replied, because a message dies with the session
that received it and this exchange has already outlived two orchestrator sessions.

THE QUESTION ASKED: how do lore users and this repository's fixtures actually name snapshots, and
are single-word names common enough that forbidding them is a real tax rather than a theoretical
one? The ruling is opum-agent's; this is the measurement, taken against lore-cli origin/dev.

THE ANSWER REFRAMES THE QUESTION: there are ZERO user-chosen snapshot names in existence, because
a snapshot cannot be named today at all.

  1. The snapshot key is a CONTENT DIGEST, enforced by schema, not a human string:
     src/core/snapshot.ts:104  const digestSchema = z.string().regex(/^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$/u);
     src/core/snapshot.ts:193  snapshotKey: digestSchema,
  2. `lore snapshot retain` ACCEPTS NO NAME. Its usage line is
     `lore snapshot <retain|list|delete> [snapshot-key]`, and the optional positional is a
     SELECTOR for list/delete, matched against that digest -- not a label supplied at retain time.
     Both documented examples are bare: `lore snapshot retain`.
  3. Every `retain` invocation in the entire repository passes no argument. Measured across test/,
     src/, docker/ and scripts/: test/snapshot-command.test.ts:40 and :80 are the only two call
     sites, both `["retain"]`.
  4. On-disk leaves are digests too: snapshotPath names files `${digestHex(snapshotKey)}.json`
     (snapshot-store.ts:239-241).

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE RULING. The cost opum-agent weighed -- "a permanent usability constraint on a
public surface: `baseline` becomes `baseline-1`" -- is a constraint on a surface THAT DOES NOT YET
EXIST. There is no `baseline` today to migrate, no fixture to rename, no user workflow to tax, and
no back-compatibility question, because ODOC-231's human-readable `<name>.json` introduces naming
to this subsystem for the first time. A rule imposed before the first name is minted costs nothing;
the same rule imposed after costs a migration.

So the trade-off that was genuinely two-sided when asked is one-sided on measurement: single-word
names are not rare here, they are IMPOSSIBLE here, and nobody has one. This repository's own
recommendation is therefore to require the hyphen and demote the reserved-name list to
defence-in-depth -- which also removes the residual risk 9c can only warn about, since every
Windows device name (present, superscript, and any future COMn) is unbroken alphanumerics and is
excluded by shape rather than by enumeration.

STATED AS A LIMIT, because it is the honest boundary of what was measured: this is lore-cli's own
repository and test corpus. It cannot see how the handful of external `@opum-ai/lore` installs name
things -- but since the CLI gives them no way to name a snapshot either, the same argument covers
them by construction rather than by sampling.

The decision remains opum-agent's and gets recorded in opum-doc. This is the evidence, not a ruling.
